sources.publisher: Internet Engineering Task Force / RFC Editor
sources.name: RFC 9204 — QPACK: Field Compression for HTTP/3
sources.role: HTTP/3 field-section compression, dynamic-table, blocked-stream and decoder-state contract
verified_facts: QPACK is a compression format for representing HTTP fields in HTTP/3.
QPACK permits out-of-order delivery while balancing compression efficiency against head-of-line blocking.
Encoder and decoder streams synchronize dynamic-table state, and invalid references or decompression failures are protocol errors.
semantic_limits: Successful QPACK decoding proves only that an HTTP field section was reconstructed according to the compression state; it does not validate message content or source authority.
Dynamic-table synchronization, field-name/value recovery and reduced blocking do not provide a cryptographic digest for the response body.
QPACK success must not create a parcel-height row without exact source bytes, immutable version, polygon, CRS, vertical datum, units, method and execution receipts.

sources.publisher: Internet Engineering Task Force / RFC Editor
sources.name: RFC 9218 — Extensible Prioritization Scheme for HTTP
sources.role: HTTP Priority header, urgency, incremental delivery and PRIORITY_UPDATE scheduling-signal contract
verified_facts: The Priority header communicates initial priority parameters in an HTTP-version-independent form.
HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 PRIORITY_UPDATE frames can reprioritize a response or push stream.
Priority signals are scheduling preferences; servers can ignore them and still successfully serve responses.
semantic_limits: Urgency or incremental priority changes transmission scheduling, not source completeness, authority or numeric accuracy.
A PRIORITY_UPDATE frame is not a receipt that all response bytes were delivered, decoded or processed.
Priority order must not be used as confidence ranking for terrain sources or parcel-height candidates.

sources.publisher: Internet Engineering Task Force / RFC Editor
sources.name: RFC 9297 — HTTP Datagrams and the Capsule Protocol
sources.role: HTTP Datagram association, unreliable delivery, Capsule TLV framing and intermediary re-encoding contract
verified_facts: HTTP Datagrams convey bidirectional and potentially unreliable datagrams associated with an HTTP request.
HTTP/3 can use QUIC DATAGRAM frames, while the Capsule Protocol can carry datagrams reliably on an HTTP data stream.
Capsules are type-length-value tuples, and their payload semantics are defined by the capsule type or using extension.
semantic_limits: Receipt of an HTTP Datagram does not prove complete application data because unreliable delivery can omit datagrams.
Capsule length and clean parsing prove framing consistency, not source authority, object digest or measurement correctness.
Intermediary re-encoding between QUIC DATAGRAM frames and DATAGRAM Capsules prevents transport encoding from being treated as immutable source identity.

sources.publisher: Internet Engineering Task Force / RFC Editor
sources.name: RFC 9220 — Bootstrapping WebSockets with HTTP/3
sources.role: HTTP/3 Extended CONNECT, WebSocket setting, pseudo-header, stream closure and cancellation contract
verified_facts: RFC 9220 adapts the Extended CONNECT WebSocket bootstrap mechanism to a single HTTP/3 stream.
SETTINGS_ENABLE_CONNECT_PROTOCOL advertises support, and the Extended CONNECT request identifies the websocket protocol.
Orderly WebSocket tunnel closure maps to HTTP/3 stream FIN, while exceptional closure maps to an HTTP/3 stream error.
semantic_limits: Successful Extended CONNECT establishes a tunnel; it does not authenticate terrain data carried inside the tunnel.
A WebSocket message or orderly FIN is not a canonical-object, source-digest or numeric-sampling receipt.
Tunnel availability and stream closure must not create a business row without exact bytes, parcel geometry, CRS, vertical datum, units, method and provenance.
